The opening claim becomes an invitation to come and see

The chapter opens with the largest claims in the book. It then turns to a simple scene. Two men ask Jesus where he is staying (verse 38). Verse 39 answers, “Come and see.” They go and stay the day. Philip uses the same words to Nathanael in verse 46. The great claim is offered as an invitation to look.
Remembering after resurrection changes understanding of the temple saying

The hearers think Jesus means the building (verse 20). Verse 21 says he meant his body. No one understood at the time, including the disciples. Verse 22 says they remembered after he was raised. Then they believed the Scripture and his word. John tells the story from that later point of view. Some sayings can be understood only after the events they point to.
A teacher's questions stand beside a witness's willingness to decrease

John’s disciples are worried about losing their following (verse 26). John answers with a wedding. The bride belongs to the bridegroom (verse 29). The friend stands by and is glad to hear the groom’s voice. John says his joy is complete. Verse 30 then states his place in one line. He was sent to point to another, so growing smaller is success.
The woman's invitation leads others to hear for themselves

The woman leaves her water jar and goes to the town (verse 28). She says, “Come, see a man” (verse 29). Many believe because of her word (verse 39). They ask Jesus to stay, and he stays two days. Verse 42 reports what they then tell her. They now believe because they have heard for themselves. Her invitation did its work by bringing them to him.
The man's lack of help leads into a dispute about work

Jesus asks the man a direct question in verse 6. The man does not say yes. Verse 7 explains why he has not been healed. He has no one to help him into the pool. Others always get there first. He has been alone among a crowd for years. Jesus heals him with a word, and the dispute turns to Sabbath work.
A meal leads to words that some followers cannot accept

Verse 60 says many disciples found the teaching hard. Verse 66 says they left and walked with him no more. Jesus asks the twelve whether they will leave too. Peter does not say he understands. Verse 68 asks where else they would go. He stays because of who Jesus is and what he has found in his words. Verse 69 adds that they have come to believe and know.
The divided crowd prevents a single response from representing everyone

This chapter shows a crowd that cannot agree. Verses 12, 40–43 record several opinions at once. The rulers want an arrest and scorn the crowd (verse 49). Nicodemus is one of those rulers. Verse 51 asks a plain legal question. Does their law condemn a man before hearing him? No single response in the chapter speaks for everyone.
Claims about ancestry meet the question of present conduct

The hearers rest their case on ancestry (verses 33 and 39). Jesus does not deny their descent (verse 37). He asks what they are doing now. Verse 40 says they seek to kill a man who told them the truth. He adds, “Abraham didn’t do this.” A family line is shown by family likeness. The words belong to one heated dispute and should not be turned against a people.
Repeated questioning gives the healed man a voice of his own

The man is questioned four times in this chapter. Each time he says a little more. He calls Jesus “the man” (verse 11) and then “a prophet” (verse 17). Verse 25 refuses to go beyond what he knows. He was blind, and now he sees. He will not call Jesus a sinner to please his judges. By verse 38 he says, “Lord, I believe.”
The shepherd's care answers the danger of abandonment

Verse 11 defines the good shepherd by one act. He lays down his life for the sheep. Verses 12–13 describe the hired man by contrast. He sees the wolf, leaves the flock, and runs. The sheep are not his, and he does not care about them. The test comes when danger arrives. Verse 18 adds that Jesus lays down his life of his own will.
Restored life produces a plan for another death

A man has been raised, and many believe (verse 45). The council treats that as a danger. Verse 48 gives their fear: Rome may take away their place and nation. Verse 50 gives the high priest’s reasoning. One death is better than the loss of all. Verses 51–52 say he spoke more truly than he knew. A gift of life leads directly to a plan for death (verse 53).
The seed image changes the meaning of royal praise

The crowd has just hailed Jesus as king (verse 13). Foreigners are asking for him (verse 21). He says the hour of glory has come (verse 23). Verse 24 then explains what that glory is. A seed stays alone unless it is buried and dies. Only then does it bear much fruit. The praise at the gate is to be read through that picture.
The teacher's lowered position supplies the example for followers

Verse 3 says Jesus knew the Father had given all things into his hands. With that knowledge he takes a servant’s towel. In verse 13 he accepts the titles Teacher and Lord. Verse 14 argues from them. If the Lord has washed their feet, they must wash each other’s. He does not give up his rank to serve. He shows what that rank is for.
Questions about departure meet a promise of continued teaching

The disciples ask three anxious questions in this chapter (verses 5, 8, 22). They fear losing him. Verse 26 promises that his teaching will continue. The Holy Spirit will teach them and remind them of his words. The Spirit’s work is tied to what Jesus has already said. Their remembering will be helped. Verse 27 follows with a gift of peace.
The vine image leads into the command to love

Verses 1–8 speak of branches and fruit. Verses 9–10 say that remaining in the vine means remaining in his love. Verse 12 then says what the fruit is. They are to love one another as he has loved them. Verse 13 measures that love by laying down one’s life. Verse 17 repeats the command. The picture of the vine leads straight to it.
Confidence about understanding meets a warning of scattering

In verses 29–30 the disciples say they finally understand. They are sure of their belief. Verse 31 answers with a question: “Do you now believe?” Verse 32 says they are about to scatter, each to his own home. They will leave him alone. Their confidence is real and not yet tested. Verse 33 gives them peace that rests on him, not on their firmness.
The prayer extends belonging beyond the people presently listening

Verses 6–19 pray for the disciples in the room. Verse 20 widens the prayer. It includes all who will believe through their word. Later readers are among those prayed for. Verse 21 asks that they all be one, as the Father and Son are one. The purpose is that the world may believe. Verse 15 says they stay in the world for that reason.
Open testimony contrasts with denial and armed force

Pilate needs to know whether Jesus is a rival to Rome. Verse 36 answers by pointing to what his followers did not do. If his Kingdom were of this world, they would fight. Jesus stopped the one sword drawn for him (verse 11). His rule does not come by force. He has also said that he spoke openly (verse 20). Peter, meanwhile, denies him in the dark (verses 17, 25–27).
The execution scene joins completed work with care for those remaining

Four soldiers are dividing his clothes (verses 23–24). Near the cross stand his mother and the disciple he loves. Verse 26 gives her a son, and verse 27 gives him a mother. From that hour the disciple takes her into his home. Jesus arranges her care while he is dying. Verse 30 then records, “It is finished.” The finished work includes this act for those left behind.
Different paths to recognition lead toward readers who have not seen

People come to recognize Jesus in different ways in this chapter. One disciple sees the cloths and believes (verse 8). Mary knows him when he speaks her name (verse 16). Thomas asks to touch and then confesses him as Lord and God (verse 28). Verse 29 blesses those who have not seen. Verse 31 says the book was written for them. The written signs are offered to readers in place of sight.
Peter's restored task does not determine another disciple's future

Peter denied Jesus three times beside a charcoal fire (18:18). Here he is asked three times beside another (verse 9). He receives a task and word of his own death (verses 18–19). Then he asks about another disciple (verse 21). Jesus says that is not Peter’s concern and tells him to follow. Verse 23 corrects a rumor that grew from this. Jesus said “if,” and people heard a promise.
